extracted.intended_audience: students, philosophers of science, and experimental researchers learning methods for inferring causation
extracted.subtask_description: Canonical methods and precautionary principles for using observation and experiment to infer causal relations (Methods of Agreement, Difference, Joint Method, Residues, Concomitant Variations, and related safeguards). Targeted at designing or evaluating inductive causal inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish that A is the cause of a, one must obtain a pair of instances which agree in every circumstance except the presence or absence of A (e.g., A B C → a b c versus B C → b c). By comparing such instances we can with certainty attribute the difference in consequence to A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best achieved by artificial experiment where a pre-existing state (B C) is known and then A is introduced rapidly so no other change occurs. Watch for the possibility that the effect was produced by the means used to introduce A rather than by A itself; if so, test by other experiments. The Method of Difference is the only direct empirical way to arrive with certainty at causes; spontaneous natural cases seldom furnish the required precise pair of instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: If multiple instances in which a phenomenon occurs all share some antecedent A, then A is connected with a by some invariable law (A is an antecedent of a) — though this establishes uniformity rather than, by itself, a causal relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful when artificial experimentation is impossible; chiefly useful to suggest which antecedent to test by the Method of Difference. It yields laws of phenomena (uniformities) but not conclusive proof of causation unless one can also produce the effect by means of that antecedent (i.e., apply the Method of Difference). It is less demanding than the Method of Difference because any instances in which the phenomenon occurs can be examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint Method (Indirect Method of Difference / Double Method of Agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two or more instances in which the phenomenon occurs have only one circumstance in common, while two or more instances in which it does not occur have nothing in common save the absence of that circumstance, then that circumstance is the effect, or the cause, or an indispensable part of the cause, of the phenomenon. (THIRD CANON.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a double employment of the Method of Agreement (first among positive instances, then among negative instances) and can convert agreement-evidence into the positive/negative instances the Method of Difference requires. It improves upon simple Agreement but is not equivalent to a direct Difference proof because one cannot ever be sure that the affirmative or negative sets truly agree only in that one circumstance. Use as a strong suggestive procedure when direct difference is impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Subduct from any phenomenon such part as is known by previous inductions to be the effect of certain antecedents, and the residue of the phenomenon is the effect of the remaining antecedents. (FOURTH CANON.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A modification of the Method of Difference: deduce the negative instance by subtracting known effects of some antecedents to leave the residual effect ascribed to the remaining antecedent(s). Requires that previous inductions (the effects already attributed) were correctly obtained—otherwise the residue inference fails. The evidence is not complete unless the remaining cause can be produced separately or its action accounted for deductively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever phenomenon varies in any manner whenever another phenomenon varies in some particular manner, is either a cause or an effect of that phenomenon, or is connected with it through some fact of causation. (FIFTH CANON.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when an antecedent cannot be wholly removed but can be modified (e.g., heat quantity, moon position). Correlated variations suggest causal connection but do not alone determine direction (common-cause confounding). One should attempt to produce the variation by means of the alleged cause to resolve direction; and, where possible, use the Method of Difference to verify the concomitance. Useful after a Difference result to determine quantitative laws relating cause and effect (e.g., proportionalities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control other antecedents (hold background conditions constant)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether variation of one antecedent produces an effect, one must endeavor to retain all other antecedents unchanged while subjecting that particular antecedent to variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This precaution is fundamental across all methods (Difference, Agreement, Concomitant Variations). Failure to control or account for other antecedents undermines inference; where direct control is impossible, use Agreement/Joint methods or seek natural cases with known preexisting circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to be able to produce the effect (establish direction of causation)
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether an invariable antecedent is a cause, or an invariable consequent an effect, we must be able, in addition, to produce the one by means of the other; at least to obtain an instance in which the effect has come into existence with no other change than the addition of the antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If production is possible, it is an application of the Method of Difference; if not, one must rely on other methods (Agreement, Concomitant Variations, Residues) and accept weaker certainty. Always prefer producing the effect experimentally when feasible to resolve causation direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling permanent causes: use modifications rather than total removal
rubrics_metrics.description: When a cause cannot be excluded or isolated (a Permanent Cause), we may still infer its effects by observing or producing modifications in it (changes in quantity or relations) and examining consequent changes in the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: heat (cannot be entirely removed from a body) — alter quantity of heat and observe expansion; moon (cannot remove moon) — use its positional variations to infer tidal effects. This motivates the Method of Concomitant Variations. Recognize limitations where modifications do not fully simulate absence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution on numerical extrapolation and need for absolute quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: When inferring quantitative laws (e.g., a is proportional to A), one must know absolute quantities of antecedent and consequent; small observed ranges of variation may fit many possible laws, and extrapolation beyond observed limits may be erroneous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume that numerical relations observed within narrow limits hold outside those limits. Verify absolute quantities where possible. Beware of misleading empirical formulae derived from limited data (historical examples: elasticity of steam, resistance of fluids). Use wider ranges of variation or independent theoretical accounts to justify extrapolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of Composition of Causes (more cause → more effect as a general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a general rule of causation, increases in the quantity of a cause are usually followed by increases of the effect; thus variations of quantity are often safely expected to produce similar variations of consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle underpins much use of Concomitant Variations (e.g., doubling A doubles a). But exceptions exist when causes change properties upon conjunction; always check by observation/experiment, and use numerical analysis to separate contributions of multiple causes (limit behavior can reveal components due to other causes).
